tenable

/TEN-uh-buhl/ - the stress falls on TEN · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Tenable means able to be defended or maintained.

Two warm winters later, the ski resort's snow-only business plan was barely tenable, and the board began pricing mountain-bike lifts.

Worked Example

The debate coach teaches positions the way climbing instructors teach holds: before you argue anything, ask what will bear your weight. 'Homework should be abolished' caves in at the first counterexample, she warns — but 'homework should be capped' has ledges everywhere: studies to cite, trade-offs to grant, replies ready for the obvious comebacks. One position is a wish; the other is tenable.

Tenable is quality control for beliefs: not proven, not fashionable — holdable. The word admits that attack is coming and promises only that the position can survive it. Tenere, 'to hold,' is the whole idea: an argument, like a hilltop or a job title, is tenable while its holder can keep it against challengers.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

defensible: Defensible is the plain twin: a position you can defend when it comes under fire. Tenable adds the note of holding on — from tenere, to hold — a job, theory, or hilltop stays tenable only while its holder keeps it, challenge after challenge, not just through one skirmish.

sound: Sound is a slightly stronger vote of confidence than tenable: it certifies the reasoning itself as sturdy throughout, joint by joint. A tenable theory may lean on disputed data and still hold the field; calling it sound vouches for the whole structure, not just its survival.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

flimsy: too weak to hold up under any real challenge

baseless: built on nothing to begin with

Where it sits · how well the position survives challenge — conceivable → tenable → airtight

conceivable vs. tenable: A conceivable idea can at least be imagined without contradiction; tenable asks it to survive contact.

airtight vs. tenable: Airtight goes past tenable: a tenable position can be defended against challenges, while an airtight one leaves no gap for a challenge to enter.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — ten

Root — ten: to hold (Latin tenere)

Suffix — -able

Suffix — -able: able to be

Put it together

Put it together: Ten (to hold, from Latin tenere) + -able (able to be) = able to be held. Tenere holds up half of English: tenants hold leases, tenure holds a post, containers hold everything else. Tenable began as a soldier's word — a fort that could be held — and marched into seminar rooms, where positions face assaults of their own.

Word Choice

academic / measured

Tenable grades a position's health: not proven, not fashionable — holdable against challenge. Jobs, theories, and defenses are tenable while their holders can keep them. Its unit-mates divide the labor: falsifiable invites the test, replicable survives the rerun, tenable survives the argument.
